problemStatement.formal: \forall f : S^2 \to \mathbb{R}^2 \text{ continuous}, \exists x \in S^2, f(x) = f(-x)
problemStatement.plain: For any continuous map from the sphere to the plane, there must be a pair of antipodal points (opposite points on the sphere) that map to the same value. We want a purely combinatorial proof using Tucker's lemma instead of algebraic topology.

Boundary parity theorem: number of complementary boundary edges is always even
Antipodal condition is necessary: constant labeling counterexample has no complementary edges

Dominant component labeling ensures both components are small at IVT zeros
